sources.quality: Report by two court-appointed examiners, contemporary to the investigation. Dutch OCR checked against parsed passages; summaries translated, no purported courtroom transcript.
limits: Methods and observations belong to the eight examined paintings; do not generalize every fake or reproduce later simplified X-ray claims.
Report combines van Meegeren’s explanation with experimental confirmation; pigment tests alone did not date these paintings.
Some color reactions alone were insufficient; isolated binder, optical comparison, cross-sections and material comparisons formed the evidence.
sources.text: Court appointed five technical experts in June1946. They examined eight pictures. Old supports and convincing cracks did not establish the top paint’s age. X-rays showed two distinct crack networks; underlying old paint had been covered. Van Meegeren described synthetic phenol-formaldehyde resin, heating and mechanical cracking. Examiners reproduced effects and compared seized materials with samples, including isolated binder and refractive indices. Cross-sections supported resin-bound upper paint. They concluded that the examined paintings could indeed be his work.

sources.locator: Printedpp247–252; PDFpp7–12, especially missing oeuvre, Italian influence, Bredius and Miedl passages
sources.quality: Art historian who interrogated intermediary Miedl; specialist retrospective account. His own interrogation is participant-linked; other reconstruction is later interpretation.
limits: 1968 retrospective account is not a contemporaneous interrogation transcript.
Psychological motives, exact dialogue, cobalt-blue shortcut and universal statements not adopted.
sources.text: Rousseau explains success through sparse knowledge of Vermeer’s early work, religious compositions fitting a proposed Italian influence, and Bredius’s endorsement. He recounts Miedl acquiring the supposed Vermeer that went to Göring and the postwar financial-collaboration arrest. Hardening medium and artificially produced age helped disguise modern manufacture.

sources.quality: Footnoted specialist research separating period criticism, material evidence, later claims and disputed retrospection.
limits: Secondary legal description uses treason broadly; narration instead says suspicion of collaboration.
Painting during the trial denotes the extended1945–47 proceedings, not proven painting in1947courtroom.
Some experts rejected the work; never claim unanimous acceptance.
sources.text: Bredius accepted Emmaus in1937 and other experts endorsed it. Van Meegeren claimed authorship after accusation over the Adulteress sale to Göring’s agent. Some continued defending authenticity. Workshop evidence and tests supported modern authorship. Later claims of having detected the fraud early are not uniformly documented; named exceptions had period records. Decoen later disputed the technical conclusions.

limits: OCR names/punctuation may be imperfect; exact dialogue excluded.
Emmaus itself was time-barred; do not say every forgery was a count in conviction.
sources.text: Fourth chamber Amsterdam court sentenced him to one year on12November1947. Report describes procuring fraud and deliberately applying a false artist’s name or mark under Art326bis. Prosecutor requested two years on29October. Emmaus was associated in indictment but time-barred. A painting made for the investigation is mentioned separately; no courtroom painting demonstration described.

sources.text: Period article reports he had been cleared of collaboration but not forgery, and scientific examinations continued. It describes his patriotic framing as his own assertion. This supports separation of the collaboration suspicion from subsequent fraud prosecution, without determining his political character.

Reported dialogue, money, authority count and psychological/motive claims excluded.
sources.text: Historical body links collaboration accusation to a supposed Vermeer sold to Göring. It reports confession, chemical and X-ray analyst testimony and one-year jail sentence. The courtroom contained paintings; the article does not document a new painting being created there.

definitions: Van Meegeren claimed the supposed Vermeer sold to Göring was his forgery, challenging the collaboration accusation.
Collaboration suspicion and later fraud prosecution are distinct; confession alone did not establish authorship or innocence.
After the war in1945, van Meegeren was arrested on suspicion of collaboration; a supposed Vermeer reached Hermann Göring through an intermediary.
Use suspicion of collaboration, not a fabricated specific treason statute, death sentence, execution deadline or direct personal sale to Göring.
Some experts resisted accepting van Meegeren’s claim to have painted the accepted Vermeers.
Not all experts accepted every painting. No invented dialogue, universal agreement or private emotions.
His religious compositions exploited uncertainty about Vermeer’s early work and fit an expected gap; Bredius endorsed Emmaus and a museum acquired it.

Specialist historical interpretation, expressed as explanatory account rather than measured psychology. Emmaus is distinct from Adulteress sold to Göring; precise acquisition/accession differences avoided.
Van Meegeren used old painting supports and hardened synthetic-resin paint, then mechanically produced cracks to imitate age.
His account was investigated and experimentally checked; no detailed recipe, exact temperatures or claim baking alone created cracks.
Court-appointed examiners found evidence of modern synthetic-resin binder in the examined paintings and compared it with his studio materials.
Not one magical spot-test: simple color reactions alone were insufficient. Binder isolation, microscopy, optical comparison and cross-section work contributed.
X-rays revealed separate crack networks in old underlying layers and later surface paint in the examined paintings.
Faithful to original report, not RKD’s simpler shorthand. Show explanatory model, not invented archival X-ray; schematic paths not exact crack geometry.
Technical examination connected the examined paintings with van Meegeren’s materials and supported his claim of authorship.
Examiners conclude could be his hand from combined evidence; not a unique chemical fingerprint or sole method identifying a person.
The collaboration case fell away, but van Meegeren was convicted of fraud and forgery in1947 and sentenced to one year.
Broad English labels summarize verdict acts. No innocence, anti-Nazi heroism, conviction for all fakes, or claim sentence was served.
He painted a new forgery in the1947courtroom before an imminent execution.
Unsupported composite dramatic retelling; period photo places demonstration in1945. Excluded.
His forgery was a patriotic plan to trick the Nazis.
Participant self-presentation not verified motive; criminal fraud and non-Nazi victims retained.
lines: To defend himself, this painter had to prove his masterpiece was a fake.
In 1945, Han van Meegeren was arrested on suspicion of collaboration. A supposed Vermeer had reached Hermann Göring, a leading Nazi, through an art dealer.
His defense was that he had painted it himself. But some experts resisted believing that their celebrated Vermeers were forgeries.
He had exploited a gap in Vermeer’s known early work. Religious paintings filled what experts expected to find. A prominent scholar endorsed one; a museum bought it.
He used old canvases, then heated modern resin-based paint until it hardened. Cracking that surface made new paint look centuries old.
But court-appointed examiners tested the materials. They found evidence of modern synthetic resin, matching materials from his studio.
X-rays revealed another problem: separate crack patterns in the old layers underneath and the newer painting above.
The evidence supported his confession. An old canvas did not make the painting an old master.
The collaboration case fell away. The fraud did not. In 1947, he was convicted of fraud and forgery, and sentenced to one year.
He had not sold a Vermeer. He had sold the belief that it was one.
objectives: Immediate defense paradox, person identified through authentic1947court photograph, not an invented event.
Explain serious collaboration suspicion and intermediary sale; no fake painting substitution for Adulteress.
Present a defense claim, not proof; authorship question remains open.
Explain why a gap and expert endorsement made Emmaus plausible; distinguish it from Göring’s painting.
Visualize old support plus new hardened paint, then mechanically generated cracks, without reenactment.
Differentiate material evidence from confession and link comparison to studio samples.
Show two schematic crack networks in separate layers; never portray as actual scan.
Resolve support-versus-paint age and authorship through combined evidence.
Give precise conviction/year/sentence, no innocence or heroic vindication.
Return the perceived masterpiece to its true author; understanding of attribution completes the paradox.
